outline.description: Introduces the Colombian petitioners, the factual timeline leading to their departure, and the path of their case through the immigration courts to the Tenth Circuit, framing the precise issues on review.
subtopics: Petitioners: Colombian family from Bogota; political activity with Liberal Party and 2022 door-to-door campaigning for Gutierrez
Jimenez’s roles: provisional law license, law student, intern with National Prosecutor’s office assisting crime victims
Property dispute with client’s ex-husband, Rafael “Don Rafa” Montanez Lancheros, alleged narco-trafficking leader
Escalating events: threatening calls; brochure saying “death to snitches from Liberal Party”; armed threats at factory; assault of employee; intimidation of child outside school
Interactions with law enforcement: local officers’ discouraging responses; prior government attempts to search/seize the property
Relocation to countryside for three weeks, then travel to the U.S. without admission or parole
Procedural history: DHS charges; IJ finds removability and denies asylum, withholding, and CAT; BIA affirms; scope of appeal limited to asylum and withholding
Issues preserved on appeal: past persecution; nexus to political opinion; well-founded fear with government unable/unwilling; CAT and due process not pursued

outline.chapter_title: Jurisdiction, Review, and Governing Asylum Framework
outline.description: Explains the court’s jurisdiction, the deferential substantial-evidence standard, and the statutory and regulatory elements for asylum and withholding, including burdens of proof and mixed-motive principles.
subtopics: Jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252 to review final orders of removal and consolidated asylum review
Record-based review: limitation to the administrative record
Scope of review when BIA issues a streamlined affirmance; ability to consult IJ’s reasoning
Substantial-evidence standard for factual findings; when reversal is compelled
Asylum eligibility: definition of refugee under § 1101(a)(42)(A); applicant’s burden under § 1158(b)(1)
Past persecution as path to presumption of future persecution; three elements (harm rising to persecution; nexus to protected ground; state action or inability/unwillingness to control)
Mixed-motive rule: protected ground must be at least one central reason; political opinion cannot be incidental or tangential
Withholding of removal’s higher standard compared to asylum

outline.chapter_title: Past Persecution: Threats, Psychological Harm, and Cumulative Assessment
outline.description: Analyzes whether the petitioners’ experiences constitute past persecution under Tenth Circuit standards, considering both individual and cumulative harms.
subtopics: Persecution concept: more than mere restrictions or threats; offensiveness and severity requirement
Evidence presented: repeated threats; armed confrontations; brochure; assault of employee; child intimidation; absence of actual physical injury to petitioners
Petitioners’ claims of emotional and psychological harm (insomnia; child’s panic attacks)
Cumulative-evidence approach vs. isolated incidents
Tenth Circuit guidance: threats alone typically insufficient; physical harm not required but severity matters
Comparative case references: Karki; Brandy; Chhetri; Carias-Mejia
Holding on this element: substantial evidence supports BIA’s finding that, even in the aggregate, the harms did not rise to persecution

outline.chapter_title: Nexus: Political Opinion Versus Personal Retaliation
outline.description: Evaluates whether the harm was inflicted on account of petitioners’ political opinion, distinguishing political motives from personal or criminal retaliation tied to Jimenez’s legal activities.
subtopics: Protected grounds at issue: political opinion; abandonment of particular social group argument on appeal
Legal test: political opinion must be at least one central reason; treatment of mixed motives
Record evidence of motive: initial generic political threats vs. later specific threats post–property dispute
Statements by perpetrators labeling Jimenez a “snitch” for prosecutor’s office and blaming him for searches/seizures
Temporal and causal link to Don Rafa’s property and criminal enterprise; lack of evidence tying Don Rafa to early political threats
Court’s conclusion: predominant motive was personal/professional interference with criminal operations; political opinion was tangential or subordinate

outline.chapter_title: Government Unable-or-Unwilling Requirement and Internal Relocation
outline.description: Addresses whether the Colombian government was unable or unwilling to protect the petitioners and whether safe internal relocation within Colombia was feasible and reasonable.
subtopics: Unable-or-unwilling framework: government efforts to stop persecutors and to protect the applicant; importance of notice and reporting
Petitioners’ limited outreach to authorities: informal conversations with two officers; no formal reports despite government affiliations
Futility/danger exception to reporting and why the record did not substantiate it here
Countervailing evidence: prior government searches/seizures of the property undermining claim of government complicity
Conclusion on government protection: substantial evidence supports finding that government could have acted if properly notified
Internal relocation standard: government may rebut fear via safe relocation showing
Evidence supporting relocation: family remaining unharmed in Colombia; three-week safe stay in countryside; threats directed at leaving neighborhood, not country
Result: even assuming fear, record supports feasibility and reasonableness of relocating within Colombia

outline.chapter_title: Disposition, Withholding of Removal, and Key Takeaways
outline.description: States the court’s final decision and distills practical lessons about evidence and argumentation for asylum and withholding claims.
subtopics: Disposition: petition for review denied
Asylum failure on multiple independent grounds: no past persecution; no nexus to protected ground; no showing of government inability/unwillingness; safe relocation available
Withholding of removal: necessarily fails given asylum failure and its higher standard
Unappealed issues: CAT and due process claims not before the court

Practice lessons: document severe harm beyond threats; develop concrete evidence linking persecutor’s motive to a protected ground; report to authorities or substantiate futility/danger; corroborate government complicity with systemic, not anecdotal, evidence; address internal relocation with specifics
